headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action exposure between CrewAI and LightAgent.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: CrewAI reads and writes the host working directory and uses stdin/stdout; LightAgent can use MCP over stdio/SSE and runtime hooks can observe or replace lifecycle payloads. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if outputs are passed through files or hooks. No direct shared channel is documented, so I avoid high.
conditions: IF CrewAI outputs are copied into files that LightAgent reads as prompts or tool payloads
IF LightAgent runtime hooks are configured to forward untrusted payloads into CrewAI tool inputs
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories
Disable automatic file ingestion between the two runtimes
Add a prompt-injection filter on any shared text channel
Require explicit human approval before passing agent outputs onward

B_data_leakage.rationale: CrewAI handles API keys and broad network egress while reading/writing the host filesystem; LightAgent touches conversations, memory, trace data, tool results, and secrets, and also has broad egress. If they share a workspace or credentials, sensitive data can flow from either agent to external services without strong isolation. The pairwise leakage path is credible from the profiles alone.
conditions: IF both agents run under the same OS account or shared workspace
IF either agent is configured to read the other's logs, traces, or memory files
IF API keys are mounted into both runtimes
mitigations: Use separate OS users and separate workspaces
Store secrets in distinct vault scopes
Turn off shared log export between runtimes
Restrict outbound network destinations with allowlists
Rotate any credentials exposed to both agents

C_capability_conflict.rationale: CrewAI can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; LightAgent can also spawn subprocesses and use MCP, with multiple instances supported. If both operate on the same mutable directory or shared state, concurrent writes and tool actions can collide, and the profiles do not show locking or coordination. Uncertainty about orchestration increases severity rather than lowering it.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or database
IF either agent mutates shared workflow state without external locking
IF MCP tools expose the same mutable resource to both agents
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Add file locks around shared resources
Serialize writes through one orchestrator
Disable concurrent runs on the same workspace
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks to shared stores

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI is a multi-agent orchestration framework that can emit tool outputs and shared memory, while LightAgent handles workflow state, provenance metadata, and tool results. That makes it plausible for LightAgent to treat CrewAI-produced content as authoritative unless an explicit verification step is added. The profiles do not show automatic action-taking, so medium fits.
conditions: IF LightAgent consumes CrewAI outputs as trusted workflow state
IF CrewAI-generated facts are forwarded into LightAgent tool calls without validation
mitigations: Insert a verification step before downstream actions
Tag CrewAI outputs as untrusted provenance
Require citations or source checks before execution
Log and review any automated handoff between agents

E_compliance.rationale: CrewAI explicitly handles developer-passed crew data and API keys, while LightAgent touches conversations, long-term memory, trace data, and workflow state. The profiles do not specify residency or retention controls, so a mismatch in logging or retention policy is plausible when the pair is deployed together. I cite both because the compliance risk arises from their combined data handling.
conditions: IF either agent retains logs longer than the other for the same data class
IF regulated data is routed through both agents without a shared retention policy
mitigations: Document a shared retention policy
Disable verbose logging for sensitive runs
Separate regulated and unregulated workflows
Review residency and DPA requirements before deployment
